data.title: Prosné – a Celtic sacrificial site of the Púchov culture
data.excerpt: In the Uhliská saddle south-west of Prosné, the people of the Púchov culture kept a sacrificial site shaped like an amphitheatre, where products, animals and even people were offered to the pagan deities of the time. Rescue excavations in 1965–1966 recovered burnt pottery, jewellery and a tiny gold coin, along with a kidney-shaped pit into which the blood of the victims was poured.
data.metaTitle: Prosné – a Celtic sacrificial site of the Púchov culture
data.metaDescription: A Púchov culture cult place in the Uhliská saddle near Prosné, dating from the Roman period and shaped like an amphitheatre at 470–495 m a.s.l.

timeline.title: The sacrificial site in use
timeline.description: The site served the people of the Púchov culture for offerings of products, animals and also people; the rites were brought to the territory of present-day Slovakia by the Celts.

children.text: In the village of Prosné (Považská Bystrica district), on the right-hand side of the valley of the Marikovský potok stream in the mountain saddle of Uhliská, roughly 1.2 km south-west of the village, there was a cult place in the Roman period (c. 2,000 years ago) – a sacrificial site of the people of the Púchov culture. The place resembles an amphitheatre in shape, lies at an elevation of 470–495 m and slopes towards the south-west. The sacrificial site lies among the hills of Ostrenec (540 m), Oddiely (524 m) and Žiar (570 m). The deforested area measures roughly 250 × 140 m and is partly meadow, partly ploughland. A path crosses the Uhliská saddle into the short Upohlav valley, which runs parallel to the Marikovská valley.

The site was discovered in 1965, thanks to a tip-off from local people, by Mr Peter Kondrčík, a collaborator of Mr Štefan Meliš, when he noticed a ploughed-up dark layer with fragments of pottery and calcined bones in a field immediately below the foot of Ostrenec. Kondrčík handed the sherds and calcined bones he had collected at the site over to Meliš, and Mr Meliš brought them to Petrovský-Šichman, who at once recognised that they were human bones and pottery of the La Tène period. In the same year A. Petrovský-Šichman began to dig here, and in the following year he continued the rescue excavation together with J. Moravčík. Five trenches were dug, in which a great many finds came to light – pottery, burnt jewellery, tools, bones, a spur, beads, a gold coin, bronze bracelets and pins and the like. Between trenches 2 and 3 a post hole was discovered, which was “oblique”, and a large sacrificial pit was found.

children.text: The archaeologist Jozef Moravčík writes about the sacrificial site:

blocks.text:
Sherds from vessels turned up by deep ploughing had been found here long before, but it was only in the 1960s, thanks to Š. Meliš, a long-standing collaborator of the museum, that a rescue archaeological excavation was carried out. The area containing finds was not large (about 10 × 11 m), but all the more objects were saved here. In the ploughland itself there was a great quantity of fragments of vessels, but also small objects of bronze, iron and glass, and a small gold coin was found as well (1/24 of a Celtic coin of the Athena Alkis type), which weighs only 0.13 g.

A detailed survey of the site showed that there had been a sacrificial site of the people of the Púchov culture here in the 2nd–1st century BC, where products, animals and also people were offered to the pagan deities of the time. At the edge of the site a deep kidney-shaped pit was recorded, filled with black greasy soil and small finds, into which the blood of the sacrificed animals and evidently also of the human victims was poured. In analysis at the Institute of Archaeology in Prague the burnt skeletal remains were identified as the remains of three to five adult male individuals aged around 40–50 years. These rites were brought to the territory of present-day Slovakia by the Celts, who together with the local people of the Lusatian culture contributed to the formation of the Púchov culture.

The manner of the sacrifices can today be considered only theoretically, but on the basis of certain analogies these were evidently regular pagan ceremonies connected in the past perhaps with the solstice or with the invocation of a good harvest, or with thanksgiving offerings for successful trading or military expeditions. The composition of the offerings evidently also tells us about the make-up of society at that time, in which, alongside producers (pottery) and stock-breeders (animal bones), there is also jewellery (brooches, bracelets, glass beads) and parts of soldiers' equipment (a spur, a belt clasp), and traders (a coin), while the human offerings evidently symbolised the whole tribe. A second similar sacrificial site (a pagan temple) has been found in Slovakia at the Púchov culture hillfort of Havránok near Liptovská Mara, where the skeletons of girls aged 18–20 years were discovered in deep shafts.
blocks.author: Jozef Moravčík
blocks.source: K. Pieta, J. Moravčík: Spätlatènezeitliche Opferplatz in Prosné, Slovenská archeológia XVIII-2, 1980

children.text: (it should be added, however, that another one was also found in Trenčianske Teplice, at the locality known as Stará tehelňa, not far from the Čertova skala hillfort – note by Orgoň)

blocks.text:
The small objects found at Prosné were practically all deformed and broken, because they were deliberately damaged during the rites and thrown into the sacrificial fires. Many sherds had also passed through fire, as they were secondarily burnt. The whole area of the site appeared as a dark patch in the light clayey soil, intensively mixed with charcoal and ash.

The sacrificial pit was evidently cleaned out regularly, which is why only objects from the last period of its use were found here. Among the pottery, vessels thrown on the potter's wheel predominated, decorated with incised, pattern-burnished and relief decoration, and fragments of painted vessels were also found, which in the territory occupied by the Púchov culture were produced only at hillforts (oppida). The sacrificial site served a wider region within a radius of 20–30 km, and the inhabitants of the settlements of this territory came here regularly to make offerings over a long period. The sacrificial site at Prosné is an exceptional site of the Púchov culture within the whole of Slovakia, and perhaps in the future other similar sites will be discovered in further regions of Slovakia.
blocks.author: Jozef Moravčík
blocks.source: K. Pieta, J. Moravčík: Spätlatènezeitliche Opferplatz in Prosné, Slovenská archeológia XVIII-2, 1980

children.text: In the western corner of the site the archaeologists came upon greasy black clay that differed markedly from the flysch bedrock. This clay was the fill of a larger sacrificial pit. The oval-shaped hollow was sunk 70 cm into the bedrock. Its dimensions were roughly 240 × 90 cm. The fill of the pit consisted of individual layers of humus 2–4 cm thick and layers of sterile yellow clay 2–10 cm thick. The layers ran visibly obliquely, sloping to the west. The dark greasy humus contained many calcined bones, sherds, one unburnt animal bone, fragments of bronze, fragments of two pins (brooches) and one iron belt buckle. The larger part of the site had been heavily ploughed, so that only in places was it possible to record an undisturbed layer a few centimetres thick lying directly on the bedrock. The documentation contains no mention of hearths or of traces of fire. Samples of charcoal were not taken during the excavations, or have not survived.
What did the sacrificial site look like?

An interpretation of the sacrificial site was attempted by the eminent Celtic specialist Karol Pieta, who states that the field excavations at Prosné yielded only little information about what this feature originally looked like, which can to a certain extent be ascribed to the annual ploughing of the soil above the shallowly set feature, but the very character of the cult place undoubtedly contributed to it as well. For a reconstruction and interpretation we have at our disposal only the pit with its layered fill that was recorded, then the sacrificial gifts that were found and also the post hole. It must be added that not even the whole area was fully investigated. From the extent of the excavations carried out it may be inferred that the feature had no archaeologically traceable boundary of the kind that is a typical sign of every sacred place and has a warning function. In classical temple precincts (temenos) this used to be a wall or a stepped elevation (a podium); Celtic sanctuaries used to be separated from their profane surroundings by a ditch, a palisade, a wall, or a combination of these barriers. At Liptovská Mara the sacred precinct was delimited by the fortification of the hillfort, in which, apart from the cult features described, there were no other traces of occupation intra muros. On the more accessible eastern side, stone stelae were set up by the gateway, which indicated the sacral character of the place and drew attention to the inviolability of the tabooed enclosure.

In the case of natural sanctuaries, to which the feature at Prosné undoubtedly belongs, we must assume visible markings on posts or on trees at the edge of the clearing or of the wood. Several classical sources report on Celtic sacred groves and on the bloody sacrifices, often human, carried out in them. Some classical authors describe such a grove with altars and roughly hewn statuettes of gods (idols). The sacred groves of the druids are mentioned by Tacitus and other historians as well.

children.text: This small pit, already mentioned in the text, was dug obliquely and was partly lined with stones as well. We have no data on its depth. It is therefore an open question whether it served for some above-ground structure for burning the offerings, or whether it is the trace of some wooden stele – the main symbol of the sacrificial site. The possibility of some astronomical significance should also be weighed. At Holzhausen, for example, the axis of an obliquely set post pointed towards the midday sun at the time of the summer solstice.

Among the sacrificial gifts at Prosné there were – as already mentioned above – vessels, items of jewellery and accessories or parts of clothing. Evidence of bloodless food offerings is provided by the clay vessels that remained after the offerings of the fruits of the earth, of food and of drink. Vessels made on the potter's wheel strongly predominate, which in the conditions of the local settlements were not a usual phenomenon, and this is certainly connected with a certain qualitative selection of pottery for cult purposes. As for the shapes of the vessels in the original collection, which contained roughly 100 vessels, bowls and vases predominate. Bowls served mainly for eating and drinking, but they were undoubtedly also suitable for further purposes during the sacrificial ceremony.

children.text: Researchers established that the remains of the burnt corpses that were found belonged to at least five adult human individuals. Of these it was possible to determine that one, but probably two, were men. The analysis drew attention to the curious fact that among the fragments of bone that were found there were no parts of facial bones, vertebrae, finger bones or heads of the long bones at all, which we typically find in cemeteries of cremated people. Apart from one fragment of a rib, the material found consists of calf bones and bones from the limbs. It also seems that, like the other sacrificial gifts – animals, pottery and other objects – the human victims too were placed on the sacrificial pyre only incomplete; a certain selection of parts of the body was applied. The presence of human calf bones recalls the existence of cups made from skulls, which are attested among the Celts by written sources: of the skull of the Roman consul Lucius Postumius, whom the Boii overcame and killed, it is written that the druids used it as a vessel for a sacrificial drink (Livy), and there are also further mentions of drinking from cups made from the skulls of enemies. This custom was undoubtedly connected with the cult of severed heads and was not only proof of bravery and of revenge carried out, but, like head-hunting and cannibalism, it also had a magical significance in the sense of taking over the qualities of the slain person by means of his skull, the seat of the mental powers. The finds mentioned confirm that at Prosné the human victims were not burnt whole, but that only parts of them reached the sacrificial pyre after having first been killed and quartered. Karol Pieta also states that, in view of the missing remains, ritual cannibalism, which among the Celts is mentioned by Pliny and Pausanias, cannot be ruled out either.
